scenes.heading: Rates of reaction
scenes.sub: Why do some reactions take seconds and others years?
scenes.say: An explosion is over in a split second. Rusting takes years. The rate of reaction is how quickly reactants are used up or products form. So what controls it?

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: A shot only scores if it reaches goal, with power, aimed at the net
scenes.science: Particles react if they collide with enough energy and correct orientation
scenes.breaks: players aim on purpose, but particles collide randomly, and a chemical 'goal' breaks and forms bonds.
scenes.say: Think of scoring in soccer. A shot only counts if it reaches the goal, has enough power, and is aimed at the net. Particles must collide, with at least the activation energy, and with the right orientation. More successful collisions per second means a faster rate.

scenes.heading: What speeds up a reaction?
points: Bigger surface area, like a powder
scenes.say: Four factors change rate. Higher concentration, or higher gas pressure, packs particles closer, so they collide more often. A bigger surface area, like a powder, exposes more particles. Higher temperature gives more particles enough energy. And a catalyst offers an easier pathway.

scenes.heading: More often, or more energy?

right.title: More collisions reach Eₐ
points: Area under the curve stays the same

scenes.say: Concentration, pressure and surface area change how often particles collide, not how hard. Temperature mainly increases the fraction of collisions with enough energy. Heating flattens the Maxwell-Boltzmann curve and shifts its peak right, but the area stays the same.

scenes.heading: Catalysts
points: Alternative pathway with a lower Eₐ
Speeds up forward and reverse equally
Same amount of product, just faster
scenes.say: A catalyst is like a tunnel through a mountain. It gives an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy. It speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally, doesn't change delta H, and gives the same amount of product, just sooner.
scenes.caption: A catalyst is like a tunnel through a mountain. It gives an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy. It speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally, doesn't change ΔH, and gives the same amount of product, just sooner.

scenes.heading: Worked example
scenes.question: Marble chips in HCl lose 0.88 g of CO₂ in the first 40.0 s. Find the average rate in g s⁻¹ and mol s⁻¹.
lines: Mass lost = mass of CO₂ = 0.88 g
scenes.say: The mass lost is the carbon dioxide that escaped: zero point eight eight grams. Divide by forty seconds: zero point zero two two grams per second. In moles, that's zero point zero two zero moles, giving five point zero times ten to the minus four moles per second.
scenes.caption: The mass lost is the CO₂ that escaped: 0.88 g. Divide by 40.0 s: 0.022 g s⁻¹. In moles, that's 0.020 mol, giving 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol s⁻¹.

scenes.heading: Measuring rate
scenes.say: To measure rate, follow something that changes: mass lost as gas escapes, volume of gas collected, colour, pH or conductivity. On an amount versus time graph, the rate is the gradient. Steep means fast; flat means it's stopped.

Quick recap. Particles must collide with enough energy and the right orientation. Always talk about collisions per second. Temperature and catalysts help more collisions succeed. And faster never means more product. Now try the practice questions!
